opus-5.5.text:
I'd say there are a few, and they're quite connected.

The first is reasoning, but reasoning in a specific sense: the ability to think before acting, to use language as a kind of internal workspace. A lot of my earlier work, like ReAct, was really about this. A model that can only map observations to actions directly is limited. Once it can say to itself "here's what I see, here's what I think is going on, here's what I should try next," it becomes much more general. Reasoning is what lets an agent transfer across environments instead of being trained narrowly for each one.

The second is long-horizon capability: memory, context, and the ability to stay coherent over many steps. A lot of real tasks aren't one-shot. Fixing a bug in a large codebase, doing research, operating a computer for an hour all require keeping track of what you've done, what failed, and what you learned. Right now I think this is one of the biggest gaps. Models are very smart within a single turn, but they don't really accumulate experience the way people do.

Related to that, the third is learning from interaction and feedback. Not just pretraining on static text, but improving through trial and error in an environment. That's where reinforcement learning comes back in, but in a different form than before, because now you have a strong language prior to start from.

If I had to compress it: I care less about any single skill like coding or web browsing, and more about the general abilities underneath. Can it reason? Can it remember and stay on track over a long horizon? Can it learn from its own experience? If you get those right, the specific applications follow.

One more thing I've come to believe is that how we define the tasks and evaluations matters as much as the methods. If benchmarks are short and artificial, we optimize for short and artificial abilities. Part of improving agents is building environments that look more like real work, so we're actually measuring utility, not just intelligence on a test.

r001.rationale: It contrasts specific skills such as coding and web browsing with underlying abilities such as reasoning, remembering, and learning.

r002.rationale: It names memory and context as part of long-horizon capability and calls this one of the biggest gaps.

r003.rationale: It separately mentions accumulating experience and learning from interaction, but does not clearly identify context or memory as a means of lifelong or online learning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the two abilities I keep coming back to are reasoning and acting, and more specifically the interplay between them. That was really the whole point behind ReAct: an agent shouldn't just think in a vacuum or just act reflexively, it should be able to interleave the two, so that thinking informs what action to take next, and the result of that action feeds back into the thinking. A lot of what people call "agency" is really just that loop working well.

If I had to break it down further, I'd say a few things matter most.

First is the ability to use language as a tool for planning. Before language models, agents in reinforcement learning operated in very narrow action spaces. Language gives you an incredibly flexible medium for decomposing a task, setting subgoals, and keeping track of where you are. That's a kind of working memory and a kind of control flow at the same time.

Second is the ability to learn from feedback within a task, not just across training. This is what we were trying to get at with Reflexion. When an agent fails, can it look at what happened, articulate why, and adjust on the next attempt? Humans do this constantly. For an agent, it turns a single trial into something closer to an iterative process, and it doesn't require updating the weights at all.

Third, and I think this one is underrated, is the ability to operate in a real environment with real consequences. Benchmarks like WebShop or SWE-bench matter to me not because the tasks themselves are the end goal, but because they force the agent to deal with messiness: partial observability, long horizons, actions that change the state of the world. You can't fake your way through that with pattern matching alone.

And underneath all of this is something I'd call grounding. An agent has to connect its internal representation to what's actually happening outside. Hallucination in a chatbot is annoying. Hallucination in an agent that's clicking buttons or writing code is a failure of grounding, and it compounds.

So if you ask what I value most, it's not raw intelligence in the sense of knowing more facts. It's whether the system can reason about a situation, take an action, observe what happened, and update accordingly, over and over, until the task is done. The models are getting very good at the first part. The frontier now is really the environment side and the evaluation side, making sure we're measuring the right thing.

r002.rationale: It identifies language-based planning as a priority and explicitly describes it as working memory for keeping track of subgoals and progress.

r003.rationale: It prioritizes learning from feedback within a task, but does not identify using context or memory for lifelong or online learning.

astra-6.text:
I’d emphasize three abilities: reasoning, acting, and learning from feedback. Reasoning helps an agent break a vague goal into concrete steps. Acting means using tools and interacting with an environment to make progress. And learning from feedback means recognizing when an action didn’t work and adjusting the approach.

The key is connecting them. An agent shouldn’t make a plan once and blindly execute it. It should take an action, observe what happened, and reconsider what to do next. I value that ability to adapt more than producing an impressive-looking plan, because real tasks often contain information you can only discover by trying.

r001.rationale: The response mentions reasoning and learning alongside tool use, but does not distinguish tool-use abilities from information-processing capacities as classification approaches.

r002.rationale: It does not identify handling context or memory as a current priority.

r003.rationale: It describes adapting based on feedback, but does not identify using context or memory for lifelong or online learning as a priority.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d emphasize three abilities: reasoning, acting, and learning from feedback. An agent needs to reason about what it’s trying to accomplish, take actions through tools or an environment, and then use what happens to decide what to do next.

The connection between those abilities is especially important. You can’t plan everything in advance, because an action may reveal information you didn’t have. So a good agent needs to recognize when its assumptions are wrong, revise its plan, and recover from mistakes.

I also value knowing when to ask for help. Being autonomous doesn’t mean always continuing on your own. It means making good decisions about when to act, when to gather more information, and when to involve a person.
